section.title: The Broken Jar and the Prophet's Suffering
section.sectionRationale: A second sign act follows the potter's house: Jeremiah smashes a hardened clay jar before the elders to picture a judgment that, unlike soft clay, can never be reworked. The cost of that word falls immediately on the messenger himself, as Pashhur has him beaten and put in the stocks, and the section ends with Jeremiah's rawest confession, cursing the very day of his birth.
section.thesis: The broken jar shows a judgment now so hardened it cannot be reshaped, and the suffering that follows for Jeremiah, first public humiliation, then a private crisis of faith, shows what it costs a true prophet to carry a word the world will not hear.
section.frameNote: Four scenes: the jar shattered beyond repair in the Valley of Slaughter, the same word proclaimed in the temple court, Pashhur's violence against the prophet, and Jeremiah's confession, from fire in his bones to cursing his own birth.

units.label: The broken jar
units.note: a judgment that cannot be reshaped

verses.text: This is what the LORD says: “Go and buy a clay {{baqbuq|jar}} from a potter. Take some of the elders of the people and leaders of the priests,

and go out to the Valley of Ben-hinnom near the entrance of the Potsherd Gate. 
Proclaim there the words I speak to you,

saying, ‘Hear the word of the LORD, O kings of Judah and residents of Jerusalem. This is what the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says: I am going to bring such disaster on this place that the ears of all who hear of it will ring,

because they have abandoned Me and made this a foreign place. They have burned incense in this place to other gods that neither they nor their fathers nor the kings of Judah have ever known. They have filled this place with the blood of the innocent.
They have built high places to Baal on which to burn their children in the fire as offerings to Baal, something I never commanded or mentioned, nor did it even enter My mind.
So behold, the days are coming, declares the LORD, when this place will no longer be called Topheth or the Valley of Ben-hinnom, but the Valley of Slaughter.

And in this place I will ruin the plans of Judah and Jerusalem. I will make them fall by the sword before their enemies, by the hands of those who seek their lives, and I will give their carcasses as food to the birds of the air and the beasts of the earth.
I will make this city a desolation and an object of scorn. All who pass by will be appalled and will scoff at all her wounds.
I will make them eat the flesh of their sons and daughters, and they will eat one another's flesh in the siege and distress inflicted on them by their enemies who seek their lives.’
Then you are to shatter the jar in the presence of the men who accompany you,

and you are to proclaim to them that this is what the LORD of Hosts says: I will shatter this nation and this city, like one shatters a potter's jar that can never again be repaired. They will bury the dead in Topheth until there is no more room to bury them.
This is what I will do to this place and to its residents, declares the LORD. I will make this city like Topheth.

The houses of Jerusalem and the houses of the kings of Judah will be defiled like that place, Topheth, all the houses on whose rooftops they burned incense to all the host of heaven and poured out drink offerings to other gods.”
Then Jeremiah returned from Topheth, where the LORD had sent him to prophesy, and he stood in the courtyard of the house of the LORD and proclaimed to all the people,

“This is what the LORD of Hosts, the God of Israel, says: ‘Behold, I am about to bring on this city and on all the villages around it every disaster I have pronounced against them, because they have stiffened their necks so as not to heed My words.’”
When Pashhur the priest, the son of Immer and the chief official in the house of the LORD, heard Jeremiah prophesying these things,
he had Jeremiah the prophet beaten and put in the stocks at the Upper Gate of Benjamin, which was by the house of the LORD.
The next day, when Pashhur released Jeremiah from the stocks, Jeremiah said to him, “The LORD does not call you Pashhur, but {{magormissabib|Magor-missabib}}.

For this is what the LORD says: ‘I will make you a terror to yourself and to all your friends. They will fall by the sword of their enemies before your very eyes. And I will hand Judah over to the king of Babylon, and he will carry them away to Babylon and put them to the sword.

I will give away all the wealth of this city, all its products and valuables, and all the treasures of the kings of Judah, to their enemies. They will plunder them, seize them, and carry them off to Babylon.

And you, Pashhur, and all who live in your house, will go into captivity. You will go to Babylon, and there you will die and be buried, you and all your friends to whom you have prophesied these lies.’”

units.label: Jeremiah's confession
units.note: fire in the bones, and cursing his own birth

verses.text: You have deceived me, O LORD, and I was deceived. You have overcome me and prevailed. I am a laughingstock all day long; everyone mocks me.
For whenever I speak, I cry out; I proclaim violence and destruction. For the word of the LORD has become to me a reproach and derision all day long.

If I say, “I will not mention Him or speak any more in His name,” His message becomes a {{esh|fire}} burning in my heart, shut up in my bones, and I become weary of holding it in, and I cannot prevail.

For I have heard the whispering of many: “Terror is on every side! 
Report him; let us report him!” All my trusted friends watch for my fall: “Perhaps he will be deceived so that we may prevail against him 
and take our vengeance upon him.”

But the LORD is with me like a fearsome warrior. Therefore, my persecutors will stumble and will not prevail. Since they have not succeeded, they will be utterly put to shame, with an everlasting disgrace that will never be forgotten.
O LORD of Hosts, who examines the righteous, who sees the heart and mind, let me see Your vengeance upon them, for to You I have committed my cause.
Sing to the LORD! Praise the LORD! For He rescues the life of the needy from the hands of evildoers.
Cursed be the day I was born! May the day my mother bore me never be blessed.

Cursed be the man who brought my father the news, saying, “A son is born to you,” 
bringing him great joy.
May that man be like the cities that the LORD overthrew without compassion. May he hear an outcry in the morning and a battle cry at noon,

because he did not kill me in the womb so that my mother might have been my grave, 
and her womb forever enlarged.

Why did I come out of the womb to see only trouble and sorrow, 
and to end my days in shame?

baqbuq.gloss: A narrow-necked clay flask, named for the gurgling sound it makes when poured out. Unlike the soft, reworkable clay of the potter's wheel in chapter 18, this jar has already been fired hard; once shattered it can never be reshaped, a deliberate escalation from warning to finality.

magormissabib.gloss: Terror on every side, the new name Jeremiah gives Pashhur after his violence against the prophet. It turns Pashhur's own cruelty back on him as a prophecy of his fate, and the same phrase later becomes Jeremiah's own description of his persecutors' whispering, verse 10.

esh.gloss: Fire. Jeremiah describes God's word as a fire shut up in his bones that he cannot hold in even when he wants to stop speaking; it captures the involuntary, consuming compulsion of genuine prophetic calling, not a task he chose but a fire he cannot quench.

basic.context: Jeremiah buys a hardened clay jar and smashes it before the city's elders in the Valley of Ben-hinnom, a place so associated with child sacrifice to Baal that God renames it the Valley of Slaughter. Unlike the reworkable clay of chapter 18, this jar, once broken, stays broken, a sign that judgment has now become fixed. When Jeremiah proclaims this in the temple courtyard, the priest Pashhur has him beaten and locked in the stocks, and Jeremiah's response is some of the most anguished, honest prayer in all of Scripture, ending with him cursing the very day he was born.
basic.hermeneutics: These chapters are read as real history, an actual sign act and an actual arrest, not merely literary devices. The hardest part for modern readers is Jeremiah's raw language, 'You have deceived me, O LORD,' and his curse on his own birth; the honest answer is that Scripture includes this kind of anguished, unfiltered prayer without either excusing sin or hiding real spiritual crisis, and it does not end there, Jeremiah still proclaims God's word even in his lowest moment.
basic.originalLanguages: The jar, baqbuq, is fired hard clay, no longer reworkable like the soft clay of chapter 18, a deliberate escalation. Pashhur is renamed Magor-missabib, terror on every side, turning his cruelty into a prophecy against himself, and the same phrase later describes the whispering campaign against Jeremiah. And Jeremiah describes God's word as esh, fire, shut up in his bones, capturing a compulsion he cannot resist even when persecution makes him want to.
basic.typology: The broken, unmendable jar anticipates a judgment beyond the point of easy repentance, echoed later in the New Testament's warnings about hardened unbelief. Jeremiah's suffering for faithful speech, beaten and mocked for the word he carried, previews the far greater suffering of Christ, who was likewise struck, mocked, and rejected for speaking the truth of God.
basic.christ: Jeremiah's cry, 'I am a laughingstock all day long, everyone mocks me,' anticipates the mockery Christ endured on the cross, and his experience of a word he cannot hold in even under threat mirrors Christ's own resolute obedience to the Father's will despite anguish, seen also in Gethsemane. Yet where Jeremiah curses his own birth in despair, Christ presses through His own anguish to completion, 'It is finished,' showing the fuller obedience Jeremiah's honest struggle points toward.
basic.god: God is patient enough to keep sending warnings even to a hardened people, but just enough that some judgments do finally become fixed, like the broken jar. And God is present with His suffering messenger, not shielding Jeremiah from persecution but proving Himself 'a fearsome warrior' at his side even in the darkest hour of doubt.
basic.crossReferences: Hebrews 6:4-6 speaks of a hardness that becomes settled and resistant to repentance, echoing the unmendable jar. Matthew 27:29-31 shows Christ mocked much as Jeremiah was mocked for speaking truth. Job 3 contains a similarly raw curse on the day of birth, showing Jeremiah stands within a biblical tradition of honest lament. 1 Peter 4:12-14 encourages suffering for righteousness as something Christ Himself shared.
basic.oneStory: The broken jar and Jeremiah's suffering show that carrying God's true word in a hostile world is costly, sometimes to the point of anguish that dares to curse one's own birth. That costly faithfulness finds its full and final pattern in Christ, who bore mockery and suffering for speaking truth all the way to the cross, so that those who suffer for His name are never suffering alone.

context.literary:
The two chapters are one continuous scene with four panels. In 19:1 to 13 Jeremiah speaks in the Valley of Ben-hinnom, and the order is unusual: the long oracle comes first, 19:3 to 9, and the shattering of the jar follows, 19:10 to 11, so that the act is the exclamation mark on a speech already given. Verses 14 and 15 move him to the temple court for a short summary. Chapter 20 then splits into narrative, 20:1 to 6, a confession in two halves, 20:7 to 13, and a final lament, 20:14 to 18.

Two renamings hold the unit together. The valley will no longer be Topheth but the Valley of Slaughter, 19:6, and the priest will no longer be Pashhur but Magor-missabib, 20:3. A place and a man are given names that tell what they are. The phrase 'terror on every side' then returns in the mouth of Jeremiah's enemies, 20:10, so the name that was meant as a curse on Pashhur is turned back on the prophet.

The word 'place' is the key to chapter 19. It occurs again and again in 19:3 to 12, 'this place,' as if the valley stood for the city: the place made foreign, the place filled with innocent blood, the place that will become a burial ground. Verse 12 makes the identification explicit: the city will be made like Topheth.

The confession of 20:7 to 18 is arranged against expectation. A lament normally ends in confidence, and verses 11 to 13 do reach it, with a call to sing to the LORD. Then verse 14 begins a curse, 'Cursed be the day I was born,' and the unit ends with no resolution at all. The book leaves the praise and the despair side by side.
context.historical:
The Valley of Ben-hinnom lay to the south of the city, and by Jeremiah's day it had a terrible history. Ahaz burned incense there and sacrificed his sons in the fire, 2 Chronicles 28:3, and Manasseh did the same, 2 Chronicles 33:6. The place of burning was called Topheth, and Josiah desecrated it so that no one could sacrifice a son or daughter there, 2 Kings 23:10. Jeremiah had already confronted it in his temple sermon, 7:30 to 33. Chapter 32:35 links the sacrifice to both Baal and Molech, which fits 19:5, where the burning is for Baal.

The clay jar and the elders mattered as a public act. Jeremiah takes with him some of the elders and the leaders of the priests, so the leaders are witnesses and cannot say they were not told. The Potsherd Gate, 19:2, is named as the place where the sign is done, and its name suggests broken pottery, which is a fitting setting for a broken jar.

Pashhur son of Immer was the chief official in the house of the LORD, so he held authority over order in the temple. The stocks and the beating, at the Upper Gate of Benjamin, are an official act by a priest against a priest's son, since Jeremiah belonged to a priestly family, 1:1. The setting is probably the early years of Jehoiakim, though the text gives no date. Babylon's victory over Egypt at Carchemish in 605 BC made the prediction of 20:4 to 6 a matter of politics, not just prophecy.

The horror of 19:9, eating the flesh of children in a siege, is covenant language, Deuteronomy 28:53, and it did happen in Israel's history under siege, 2 Kings 6:28 and 29, and Lamentations 4:10 records it after the fall of Jerusalem.
context.canonical:
The Valley of Hinnom, in Hebrew ge-hinnom, becomes in Greek the Gehenna of Jesus' teaching, the picture of final judgment, Matthew 5:22 and Mark 9:43. Isaiah's closing line about corpses and an unquenched fire, Isaiah 66:24, lies behind it. Jeremiah 19 is where that association begins, with a valley of slaughter and burning. At the same time the book promises that the whole valley of the dead bodies and ashes will be holy to the LORD, 31:40.

The sign of the jar completes the sequence started at the potter's house. Psalm 2:9 says the Lord's anointed will shatter the nations like pottery, and in Revelation 2:27 Christ shares that authority with those who overcome, so the broken pot also belongs to the end of the story.

Jeremiah's confession belongs with the great laments of Scripture. Job also cursed the day of his birth, Job 3:3. Elijah, under the broom tree, asked to die, 1 Kings 19:4, and Jonah did the same, Jonah 4:3. Lamentations 3:14 echoes Jeremiah's 'laughingstock' in the voice of the afflicted man. The 'fire shut up in my bones' returns in the New Testament in Paul's 'Woe to me if I do not preach the gospel!' 1 Corinthians 9:16, and in the apostles' 'we cannot stop speaking about what we have seen and heard,' Acts 4:20. Hebrews recalls those who endured mocking, flogging, chains and imprisonment, Hebrews 11:36 to 38, and Peter tells believers not to be surprised at the fiery trial, 1 Peter 4:12.

hermeneutics.authorIntent:
The author wants hearers to see that the situation has changed. At the potter's house, the clay was still wet and the potter could remake it. In the Valley of Ben-hinnom the jar is baked hard, and the sentence is that it 'can never again be repaired,' 19:11. The elders, the priests and the people are being told that this is not another warning. It is the end of the generation's chance, and the place where their children were burned is the place where the sentence is declared.

The author also wants the reader to understand why the message was not believed. Pashhur's reaction is the reaction of an institution: the one who ought to guard the house of the LORD silences the one speaking for the LORD. Jeremiah's reply, with its new name and its naming of Babylon and exile, makes the confrontation personal and public.

Then the author lets us into Jeremiah's own heart. The confession of 20:7 to 18 is placed immediately after the stocks so that we can see the price of the sign. The prophet does not hide his anger or his weariness. The book wants readers who suffer to know that this can be said in God's presence, and also that it can come with the unquenchable conviction that he must keep speaking. It also wants those who come after the exile to know what the word cost the man who first spoke it.
hermeneutics.descriptionVsPrescription:
The sign act belongs to Jeremiah. Nobody is commanded to break a jar in a public place, and the horrors of 19:9 are a description of covenant judgment under siege, not a program. Child sacrifice is condemned in the text, 19:5, and nothing here could be used to approve it.

Jeremiah's words in 20:7, 'You have deceived me,' and his curse on the day of his birth are descriptive. They are an honest record of a prophet in despair. They are not teaching about God's character, which Scripture states elsewhere: He is not a man that He should lie, Numbers 23:19, and He cannot lie, Titus 1:2. A reader who treats 20:7 as doctrine has taken a lament for a creed.

What the passage does commend is a pattern for the person who suffers for speaking truth. He tells God what he feels and does not hide it. He keeps hold of God's presence, 'the LORD is with me like a fearsome warrior,' 20:11. He is allowed to praise in the middle of it, 20:13, and also to fall back into darkness, 20:14 to 18. The Christian is not promised stocks, but Jesus does promise that disciples will be hated for His sake, and the apostles' experience in Acts 16:24 and 25, with feet in the stocks and prayers and hymns at midnight, shows the same pattern of praise inside pain.

debates.question: What does Jeremiah mean by 'You have deceived me, O LORD'?

views.label: God overpowered him, 'enticed' him into the call
views.case: The verb in 20:7 can mean to entice or persuade, as in Exodus 22:16 of seduction and 1 Kings 22:20 to 22 of enticing Ahab. Read this way, Jeremiah complains that God was too strong for him, as the next words say: 'You have overcome me and prevailed.' He did not choose this life; he was seized.

views.label: God promised safety and it did not come
views.case: God had promised at his call that enemies would fight against him but not overcome him, 1:8 and 19. Now he is beaten and in the stocks. His charge is that the promise has failed. On this view the accusation is real and God does not reprove it, though the later promise in 15:20 and 20:11 reaffirms the commission.

views.label: The language of lament, not a theological claim
views.case: Hebrew laments often speak in stark terms, as in Lamentations 3:1 and Psalm 88. Jeremiah is not teaching that God lies but pouring out the anguish. Numbers 23:19 and Titus 1:2 tell us how to read the word.

debates.bearing: All three readings agree on what the text does: God is not offended by the complaint, and Jeremiah is not released from the call. The honesty is allowed; the work continues.

debates.question: How do the praise of 20:13 and the curse of 20:14-18 belong together?

views.label: They record two moods that coexist
views.case: The book places them side by side without comment. Faith and despair can alternate in a single day, and the text does not tidy it. Many readers value this because it does not offer a quick resolution.

views.label: The order is reversed, so the curse comes first in time
views.case: Some think the curse came from an earlier low point and was placed after the praise to leave the reader in the dark, so that the book holds the reader at the edge of the exile. The final word is not resolved.

views.label: The praise is a confident anticipation
views.case: Verse 13 speaks of the LORD who 'rescues the life of the needy' in the present tense of faith, not of present experience. The curse then shows the cost of waiting for what faith already declares.

debates.bearing: The passage teaches that faith may include both. A believer is not disloyal when the song of 20:13 and the cry of 20:14 are found in the same prayer.

debates.question: Is the judgment of the shattered jar irreversible?

views.label: Irreversible for that city and generation
views.case: The jar 'can never again be repaired,' 19:11, and the sequel is the fall of Jerusalem in 586 BC. Jeremiah 20:4 to 6 names Babylon. The sign marks the point at which judgment on the city is fixed.

views.label: Irreversible for the city, not for the people
views.case: The same book promises restoration, a new covenant and the sanctifying of this very valley, 31:31 to 40. The jar speaks of the end of the old order, not of the end of God's purposes.

views.label: A last warning that still carries a call
views.case: Verse 15 describes the people as stiff-necked 'so as not to heed My words,' which implies that heeding would have mattered, as in 18:7 to 10. On this reading the sign sharpens the appeal.

debates.bearing: The first two views fit the book's overall movement: the old Jerusalem falls, and the later chapters bring a new beginning. The third reminds us that the reason for the sign is still a call to listen.

study.originalLanguages:
The oracle of 19:3 says the news will make the ears of all who hear it 'ring.' The Hebrew verb is tsalal, to tingle, the verb of 1 Samuel 3:11 and 2 Kings 21:12. The second is from the oracle against Manasseh, so Jeremiah is deliberately recalling that earlier word and showing that it is now coming due, as 15:4 had said.

In 19:5 the BSB says that child sacrifice 'did not even enter My mind.' The Hebrew is literally that it 'did not go up on My heart,' the same wording as 7:31 and 32:35. The heart is the seat of intention, so God is saying that such a thing never formed in His will.

In 19:7 the BSB footnote notes a sound-play: the verb for 'ruin,' baqoti, from baqaq, sounds like baqbuq, the jar. Jeremiah's speech announces that the LORD will 'empty out' the plans of Judah, and the empty jar is the picture. The jar's name is often explained as imitating the gurgle of liquid poured from a narrow neck, so the very word carries the sound of pouring out.

In 19:9 the siege is described as 'siege and distress,' matsor umatsoq, the pair used for the covenant curse in Deuteronomy 28:53, 55 and 57. The sentence that the jar 'can never again be repaired' in 19:11 uses the verb rapha, to heal, so the line says it cannot be healed. This ties to the incurable wound of 15:18, to the heart that could not be healed in 17:9, and to the plea 'Heal me, O LORD' in 17:14. The theme of healing runs through all these chapters and ends here with a vessel that cannot be mended.

In 20:7 the verb for 'deceived,' pittah from pata, ranges from persuade to entice to seduce, and the last of the next verbs, 'prevailed,' is yakol, to be able. The same verb returns three times: 'I cannot prevail' in 20:9, 'we may prevail against him' in 20:10, and 'will not prevail' in 20:11. Everything turns on who is able: God prevails over Jeremiah, Jeremiah cannot restrain the word, the enemies hope to prevail over him, and God will not let them.

In 20:8 the prophet's message is 'violence and destruction,' chamas washod, the words God had used of Judah's own sin in 6:7. He is made to shout the verdict on what they do.

In 20:11 the 'fearsome warrior' is gibbor 'aritz. The root 'aritz is used in 15:21 for the 'ruthless' from whose grasp God promised to redeem him, so the word applied to Jeremiah's persecutors is claimed for his defender.

In 20:14 'Cursed' is arur, the covenant word of 17:5, while Job uses a different verb for cursing his day, Job 3:1. In 20:15 the man who brought the news is a basser, a bearer of good news, the root that gives the word for the herald of good tidings in Isaiah 40:9, so the news of a birth that should have been good tidings is cursed.

typology.type: The Valley of Slaughter and Gehenna, 19:6
typology.fulfillment: A valley where children were burned becomes a valley of slaughter and burial. In the New Testament its Greek name, Gehenna, is used by Jesus for final judgment, Matthew 5:22 and Mark 9:43. The correspondence is of place and fate: what began as a site of idolatry and killing becomes the figure of what God does with evil. The escalation is that the Valley's judgment came in history, at the fall of Jerusalem, while Gehenna speaks of the last day, Revelation 20:14. The type is limited because Jeremiah promises that the same valley would at last be holy to the LORD, 31:40, a hope the figure of Gehenna does not carry.

typology.type: The messenger beaten and bound for the word, 20:1 to 2
typology.fulfillment: Pashhur, the temple's chief officer, has Jeremiah beaten and put in the stocks at a temple gate. In the same way Jesus was struck by a temple officer, John 18:22, and flogged, Matthew 27:26. The correspondence is that the guardians of the house reject the one who speaks for the house's God. The escalation is from a prophet who is released the next day, 20:3, to the Son who is handed over to death. The type falls short because Jeremiah answers with a threat and a renaming, while Jesus answers with silence and then a prayer for His persecutors, Luke 23:34.

typology.type: The word like fire in the bones, 20:9
typology.fulfillment: Jeremiah cannot hold the word in. At Pentecost the Spirit comes as tongues like flames of fire resting on each believer, Acts 2:3, and the apostles say they cannot stop speaking about what they have seen and heard, Acts 4:20. On the road to Emmaus the disciples' hearts burn as Jesus opens the Scriptures, Luke 24:32. The word that burned in one prophet is given to a whole people. The type falls short in that Jeremiah's fire came with weariness and isolation, while the Spirit's gift is shared and sustaining.

typology.type: The warrior who stands with the persecuted, 20:11
typology.fulfillment: The LORD is with Jeremiah like a fearsome warrior, so his persecutors will stumble. In Christ the promise is carried further: 'If God is for us, who can be against us?' Romans 8:31, and the one who is at God's right hand has overcome. The correspondence is real, but the victory is not that a prophet escapes the stocks; it is that the faithful are not defeated by them. The type is limited because Jeremiah's vindication is still in the future of his own history, while the believer's rests on a resurrection that has already happened.

study.christ:
The sufferings of Jeremiah in these chapters shape the way the New Testament later tells the suffering of Jesus. The prophet is mocked all day, 'everyone mocks me,' and hunted by friends who watch for his fall, 20:7 and 10. Jesus is mocked on the cross, and those closest betray Him. The temple's chief officer has Jeremiah beaten and bound, and in the same way an officer of the high priest slaps Jesus, John 18:22. Jeremiah's sign was spoken in a valley of death and ended in a courtyard where he was arrested; Jesus' word was spoken in the temple, and He was handed over from it.

The differences are as instructive as the likenesses. Jeremiah says, 'You have deceived me,' and curses the day of his birth. Jesus in Gethsemane says that His soul is consumed with sorrow to the point of death, Matthew 26:38, and offers up prayers and petitions with loud cries and tears to the One who could save Him from death, and is heard because of His reverence, Hebrews 5:7. He feels the same weight and does not utter the curse. The angel who brought good news of great joy at His birth, Luke 2:10, is the answer to the man who cursed the bearer of good news in 20:15.

The shattered jar reaches Christ in two ways. First, He speaks of the same valley, Gehenna, as the end of unrepentant evil, Matthew 5:22, and He speaks of ruling with an iron scepter and shattering like pottery as authority received from the Father, Revelation 2:27, drawing on the second psalm. Second, He is the stone on which people fall and are broken, Matthew 21:44. The jar teaches that there is a point at which the potter's patience ends, and the New Testament names the one who carries out that judgment and who also bears it for those who turn to Him.

The place where children were burned for Baal is also a reminder of what God has not demanded. He never asked for the death of a child. Yet He gave His own Son, and the difference is that this was His own offering, not a demand laid on a worshiper, the answer to Abraham's word on Mount Moriah that God would provide the lamb. This is a connection of contrast, not allegory, and it rests on the way the New Testament reads Genesis 22.

A caution: the jar is not a coded picture of Christ's body, and Jeremiah is not a sinless forerunner. His curses and complaints are part of his humanity. What the passage gives is a recognisable pattern, the faithful messenger rejected by the guardians of the house, and a true understanding of why He had to come.
study.god:
The first thing this passage shows is how God regards child sacrifice. In 19:5 He says that He never commanded it, never mentioned it and that it never entered His mind. That is a statement of His character, as strong as any: the God of Israel does not want, and never wanted, human sacrifice. Leviticus 18:21 and Deuteronomy 12:31 say the same. The religion of the surrounding nations, which could treat a child's life as a gift to a god, is completely alien to Him.

He is just in a way that fits the crime. The valley of burnt sacrifices will be filled with the dead of Judah until there is no room, 19:11. The sentence is not random cruelty but the reflection of what was done. The renaming of the valley and of Pashhur follows the same logic: God gives names that show what a thing is.

He holds the world's powers in His hand. In 20:4 He says, 'I will hand Judah over to the king of Babylon.' Babylon is not an independent force. This is not a statement that Nebuchadnezzar is good, but that history does not slip out of the LORD's hand.

He is patient and then firm. Chapter 18 showed Him able to reshape the clay; chapter 19 shows that the time of reshaping has a limit. The same God has been warning and sending prophets, and the point of the baked jar is that His warnings are real.

He does not rebuke His servant for honesty. Jeremiah accuses Him, curses the day of his birth, and God does not answer in anger. The passage gives no immediate reply, and the answer comes in the long record of the prophet's survival and the fulfilment of the word. God allows the lament to stand in His book. For believers this is a profound comfort: God is large enough to hear our worst words and does not abandon us.

He is a God who sees the heart. Jeremiah prays to the One 'who examines the righteous, who sees the heart and mind,' 20:12, and the verse echoes 11:20. He is known as the rescuer of the needy, 20:13, and as the fearsome warrior at the prophet's side, 20:11.

For worship, this means that we can say to God what we cannot say to anyone else, and that praise and anguish may sit in the same prayer. It also means that we cannot make Him into a god of our own design. He is the God who does not want a child's life and who gave His own Son.

crossReferences.note: The oracle against Manasseh announces such calamity on Jerusalem that the news will reverberate in the ears of all who hear it, and says the LORD will wipe Jerusalem as one wipes a dish. Jeremiah 19:3 takes the same language, which shows that the sign in the valley is the long-delayed execution of the sentence passed for Manasseh's sins.

Josiah desecrated Topheth in the Valley of Ben-hinnom so that no one could sacrifice a son or daughter in the fire to Molech. The reform removed the practice but did not change the heart, and Jeremiah 19 comes after it, showing that the legal clean-up was not enough.

The same charge in the temple sermon: the high places of Topheth, sons and daughters burned, something God never commanded, and the promise that the place will be called the Valley of Slaughter. The close agreement of the two passages shows that the sign act of chapter 19 enacts what the sermon had said.

The covenant curse in which, in the siege and distress inflicted by the enemy, people eat the fruit of their own womb. Jeremiah 19:9 draws on it, and the fulfilment in the fall of Jerusalem is recorded in Lamentations 4:10.

The first of the confessions, in which Jeremiah learns of the plot against him and prays that he may see God's vengeance, committing his cause to Him. Jeremiah 20:12 repeats the prayer almost word for word, so the chapters bracket a long stretch of the prophet's trials with the same appeal.

Job curses the day of his birth and wishes that it had never been. Jeremiah 20:14 to 18 follows the same form, though with a different verb for cursing. The comparison shows that the Bible makes room for the most extreme laments and that Jeremiah stands in a tradition of the suffering righteous.

The psalmist hears the slander of many and says there is terror on every side as they conspire to take his life. Jeremiah 20:10 puts the phrase in the mouths of his enemies, so what was already a lament idiom becomes a whisper against the prophet.

The afflicted man says he has become a laughingstock to all his people, mocked in song all day long. The wording matches Jeremiah 20:7, and since Lamentations is traditionally linked with Jeremiah, readers have heard in it the same voice after the fall of the city.

Paul and Silas are placed in the inner cell with their feet in the stocks, and at midnight they are praying and singing hymns. It mirrors Jeremiah's stocks and the praise of 20:13, and shows the same pattern of faith breaking out in the middle of suffering.

Paul says he is obligated to preach and cries, 'Woe to me if I do not preach the gospel!' It echoes the compulsion of Jeremiah 20:9, where the word is a fire he cannot hold in, and shows that those called to speak for God may find the call inescapable.

Abraham is stopped from sacrificing Isaac, and a ram is provided in his place. Set beside Jeremiah 19:5, it shows that God never wanted a child on the altar. The God who stopped Abraham is the God who condemns Topheth.

study.oneStory:
The sign in the valley belongs to the old story of a land defiled by blood. The Torah said that bloodshed pollutes the land and that no atonement can be made for it except by the blood of the one who shed it, Numbers 35:33. By the time of Jeremiah the land is full of innocent blood, and the place of child burning stands as its worst expression. The story of Israel in the land, begun with Joshua, is heading to its end: a nation that was to be a light to the world has made a valley of its children.

Behind this is an older question about sacrifice. In Genesis 22 God stops the knife and provides a ram, and the Law repeats that He does not want child sacrifice, Leviticus 18:21. Judah's practice at Topheth is a denial of that revelation and of the God who gave it. The jar is the answer.

The sign also marks a turning point in the line of the persecuted prophets. Jesus says that the blood of all the prophets from Abel to Zechariah will be charged to that generation, Luke 11:49 to 51. Jeremiah is one in the line, and the beating at the Upper Gate of Benjamin is a small anticipation of what the Son would later face from the same temple authorities.

The valley is not left in shame. In the book's promise of restoration, the whole valley of the dead bodies and ashes is to be holy to the LORD and never to be uprooted or demolished, Jeremiah 31:40. The place of shame becomes holy ground, which is the pattern of the gospel. The one broken for sinners makes the broken whole.

Jeremiah's cry that he should never have been born is answered in the end by a new birth. Believers are born again, John 3:3, and the Lord says that He makes all things new, Revelation 21:5. The prophet who wished that the womb had been his grave is among those for whom God will wipe away every tear, so that there is no more death or mourning or crying or pain, Revelation 21:4. The broken jar is the end of one world; the new creation is the beginning of the next, and it does not need another valley.

quiz.q: How does the broken jar in chapter 19 differ from the clay at the potter's wheel in chapter 18?

options.text: The jar is already hardened, fired clay that, once shattered, can never be reworked, unlike the soft clay before.
options.note: This marks a deliberate escalation from a warning that could still be reshaped to a judgment now fixed.

options.text: There is no meaningful difference between the two images.
options.note: The text specifically notes the jar 'can never again be repaired,' unlike the reworkable clay.

options.text: The jar is softer than the potter's clay and easily reshaped.
options.note: The opposite is true; the jar is hardened, not softer.

options.text: The jar represents only the pottery trade, with no theological meaning.
options.note: The prophecy explicitly interprets the jar as picturing judgment on the nation.

quiz.q: Why does Jeremiah rename Pashhur 'Magor-missabib', terror on every side?

options.text: As a prophecy that Pashhur's own violence would return upon him and his household in captivity and death.
options.note: The name turns Pashhur's cruelty into a declaration of his coming fate.

options.text: Because Pashhur had shown Jeremiah great kindness.
options.note: Pashhur had Jeremiah beaten and placed in the stocks; the name is judgment, not honor.

options.text: It was simply Pashhur's family name already.
options.note: The text presents it as a new name Jeremiah gives him in response to his violence.

options.text: It described the location of the temple courtyard.
options.note: The name is about Pashhur's person and fate, not a place.

quiz.q: What does Jeremiah mean by describing God's word as 'a fire shut up in my bones'?

options.text: A compulsion to speak God's word that he cannot suppress even when persecution makes him want to stop.
options.note: Verse 9 shows Jeremiah trying to hold the message in, but being unable to bear the pressure of it.

options.text: A literal physical illness Jeremiah was suffering from.
options.note: This is figurative language for the compulsion of his prophetic calling, not a medical description.

options.text: His anger at Pashhur specifically, with no wider meaning.
options.note: The fire describes his relationship to God's message generally, not merely personal anger at one man.

options.text: A momentary feeling that quickly passed and did not return.
options.note: The imagery describes an ongoing, weary struggle, not something brief.

quiz.q: How does the chapter handle Jeremiah's raw, anguished prayer, including cursing his own birth?

options.text: It records his honest anguish without editorial correction, while showing he still returns to praising God and proclaiming His word.
options.note: Verse 13 breaks into praise even amid the lament, showing honesty and faithfulness together.

options.text: It shows Jeremiah abandoning his prophetic calling entirely after this prayer.
options.note: Jeremiah continues to prophesy in later chapters; this is a crisis, not an ending.

options.text: It presents the prayer as a model liturgical formula for regular worship.
options.note: This is personal, unfiltered lament, not a prescribed pattern for corporate worship.

options.text: It condemns Jeremiah explicitly for his words in this prayer.
options.note: The text records the prayer without an explicit condemnation, in keeping with the tradition of honest lament seen elsewhere in Scripture.

quiz.q: How does Jeremiah's suffering for speaking God's true word anticipate Christ?

options.text: Both were mocked and struck for speaking truth, though Christ's suffering fulfills and surpasses Jeremiah's in bearing the world's sin.
options.note: Jeremiah's mockery previews, in shadow, the far greater suffering Christ endured for the truth He spoke.

options.text: There is no meaningful connection between Jeremiah's suffering and Christ's.
options.note: The New Testament pattern of righteous suffering for truth directly echoes passages like this one.

options.text: Jeremiah's suffering was worse than Christ's in every respect.
options.note: Scripture presents Christ's suffering, bearing the sin of the world, as the fuller and greater fulfillment.

options.text: The connection is only that both men lived in the ancient Near East.
options.note: The connection is theological, mockery and suffering for faithfully speaking God's truth, not merely historical setting.

questions: The jar, once broken, could not be repaired. Is there an area of your life where you have let hardness set in that you need to bring to God now, before it becomes fixed?
Pashhur used his position of religious authority to silence Jeremiah rather than heed him. Where might you be tempted to silence an uncomfortable truth rather than examine it honestly?
Jeremiah could not hold in God's word even when it cost him dearly, calling it 'a fire shut up in my bones.' What is God calling you to say or do that you have been suppressing out of fear?
Jeremiah brought his rawest despair honestly to God rather than hiding it. Where do you need to bring your own honest anguish to God rather than pretending it is not there?
Even in his darkest prayer, Jeremiah still breaks into 'Sing to the LORD! Praise the LORD!' How might praise and honest lament coexist in your own walk with God this week?

translationNotes.note: The word for 'jar', baqbuq, is an onomatopoeic Hebrew word imitating the gurgling sound of liquid poured from a narrow-necked flask; some versions render it 'flask' or 'bottle'.
Magor-missabib, 'terror on every side,' is a Hebrew phrase that appears again in Jeremiah's own confession, verse 10, linking Pashhur's fate to the very persecution Jeremiah himself experiences.

This closing lament has strong parallels to Job 3:1-10; both passages curse the day of birth as an expression of extreme anguish, a recognized form of honest complaint within Israel's wisdom and prophetic tradition, not a doctrinal statement about the value of life.
